title: When the wind stopped
hookLine: baby Hanuman leaps for the sun, and the wind god takes the breath out of the world
carry: the breath is prana, the life in everything

lines: A BABY JUMPS FOR THE SUN.
cards: A baby wakes up hungry, sees the rising sun, red and round, and thinks it's a fruit. So he jumps for it. This baby is Hanuman, son of the wind, and his jump carries him high into the sky.
Indra, king of the gods, sees a child rushing at the sun and strikes him with his thunderbolt. The baby falls onto a mountain, his jaw broken.
And his father, Vayu, the wind, gathers him up, carries him into a cave, and stops moving.

teach.b: This is from the Ramayana, told late in the epic by the sage Agastya. When the wind stops, everything stops with it. In the telling, no creature can breathe; bodies grow stiff as wood.

The gods hurry to Brahma, and Brahma goes to the cave himself. He touches the child, and Hanuman comes back to life. The gods shower him with blessings, and a name sticks: Hanuman, from hanu, the jaw that was struck.
Then Vayu moves again, and the whole world breathes. Here's the teaching under the story. In Hindu thought, breath isn't just air.
It's prana, the life-force that moves through every living being.

teach.h: PRANA: THE HUB OF THE WHEEL.
teach.b: The Prashna Upanishad says everything rests on prana the way spokes rest in the hub of a wheel. Hanuman's story turns that into a picture: take away the wind, and nothing lives.
That's why breath practice is a sacred practice in Hinduism, not only a way to relax. Pranayama means working with prana; ayama is a stretching, or a restraining.

teach.h: PLACE, TIME, NUMBER: LONG AND SUBTLE.
teach.b: Patanjali's Yoga Sutra watches it closely: the breath going out, coming in and held still, each observed by place, by time and by number, until it grows long and subtle.
So when someone in a Hindu home sits before puja and breathes slowly, they aren't only calming down. They're tending the gift the whole world went without, the day the wind stopped.

how: Many Hindus sit for a few slow breaths, pranayama, before puja or japa, treating the breath as prana, the life-force; some teachers shape the practice with Yoga Sutra 2.50's measures of place, time and number.

o: breath honored as prana, the life-force in every being
breathing as hard and deep as the lungs allow
a breathing trick for calming down, nothing more

games.q: the wind and the breath — tap the pairs.

s: pranayama is just a relaxation technique
in Hindu practice it works with prana, the life-force; calm comes with it, but it isn't the whole point.
in the Ramayana, when Vayu stopped moving, no creature could breathe
the gods went to Brahma, who revived Hanuman, and the wind blew again.
Yoga Sutra 2.50's goal is simply the longest breath possible
it says the breath becomes long and subtle; fine, not only long.

games.q: your aunt sits for a minute of slow breathing before she lights the lamp at puja. your little cousin asks why she doesn't just start. what fits today's story?
o: the breath is prana, the life in her, so she tends it before offering anything.
it's a warm-up, like stretching before a run.
she's just waiting for the house to go quiet.
games.why: in Hindu thought the breath is prana; Hanuman's story shows the world stopping without it. tending it before worship is part of the worship.

practice: Sit the way you would before puja, or simply upright. Find where you feel the breath most, the nose, the chest or the belly, and count the in-breath and the out-breath until they're equal.
Take six rounds on your fingers, and let only the time stretch, one count longer each way.
When the rounds are done, let go of the counting; if you pray, give thanks for the breath, and if you don't, just notice it's been moving all along without your asking.

wordCard.voice: Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, why they're sacred: the breath is prana, the life Vayu gave back to the world, watched by place, time and number.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: prana, the life-breath, the force that moves through every living being.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: the breath is prana, the life in everything. The day the wind stopped, so did the world. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda 35–36 (Agastya tells of Hanuman's childhood); also Kishkindha Kanda 66
